claims.text: Molecular dynamics simulations using specifically parameterized interatomic potentials can be used to study the thermal response of FeCuCrCoNi high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
The thermal response of FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles depends on nanoparticle size.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles have lower melting temperatures than larger FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles.
Phase transformations begin at lower temperatures in smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles than in larger ones.
The synthesized FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles have a chemically disordered, multielement nanoscale configuration.
Controlled thermal ramping in molecular dynamics can reveal thermally induced structural changes in these nanoparticles.
Surface-to-volume ratio and atomic-scale surface restructuring mediate nanoparticle phase-transformation and melting behavior.
Decreasing nanoparticle size increases the proportion of atoms located at the surface.
Surface atoms experience weaker bonding than atoms in the nanoparticle interior.
Surface atoms have increased mobility relative to atoms in the nanoparticle interior.
Weaker bonding and increased surface-atom mobility cause earlier melting and structural rearrangement in smaller particles during thermal ramping.
Bulk FeCuCrCoNi under similar thermal conditions has a higher melting point than FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles.
The melting point of bulk FeCuCrCoNi is relatively invariant compared with the size-dependent melting point of nanoparticles.
The quantitative predictions are limited by the accuracy of the interatomic potential.
The magnitude of melting-point reduction and the phase-transition temperatures are model-dependent.
The onset of melting can be operationally identified from liquid-like diffusion behavior.
Radial distribution functions or common-neighbor analysis can be used to characterize structural changes during heating.
